extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for how to observe, describe, abstract, and form general conceptions that support sound induction; explains the roles of hypothesis/colligation, measurement, and the requirements for clear and appropriate concepts. Aimed at people learning to perform and evaluate inductive inference in science and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate perception versus inference in observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic of observation consists solely in a correct discrimination between that in a result of observation which has really been perceived, and that which is an inference from the perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation extends only to sensations by which we recognise objects; propositions relate mostly to objects. In every act of observation there is at least one inference (e.g., from sensations to the presence of an object, from marks to the entire phenomenon). Analysts must separate raw sensed content from inferential claims when recording or using observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that descriptions necessarily assert resemblances beyond raw perception
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to express in words any result of observation without asserting a resemblance between the observed fact and other things denoted by the terms used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing something (e.g., 'I see something white') not only records sensation but classifies it and asserts similarity to other things called 'white.' Descriptions therefore introduce conceptual content and are not mere transcriptions of perception; be explicit about the classificatory assumptions embedded in descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat measurements as deductive conclusions, not immediate perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurements (e.g., 'ten feet long') are not immediate perceptions but conclusions from reasoning that use instruments and mathematical propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that measuring involves premises (rules of arithmetic, congruence) and that the measured fact is the result of deductive inference from observed minor premises plus mathematical truths. Record the measurement method and its inferential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use aggregation of multiple instances to reduce error in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition collected from particulars may be more certainly true than any one particular because individual instances each involve inference that may err, but collective agreement across many instances can eliminate chance error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer conclusions supported by many independent instances; assess sufficiency of sample size to 'eliminate chance.' Note that aggregation increases reliability when errors are independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat hypothesis/colligation as subsidiary to induction (not identical with it)
rubrics_metrics.description: The colligation of facts by means of hypotheses (or conceptions) is a preliminary or subsidiary operation to induction, not induction itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses to connect observed facts and identify agreements, but distinguish hypothesis-generation/guessing and subsequent verification from genuine induction (which generalizes to unobserved instances). Kepler's ellipse is an example of colligation that supplied the type for induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Method of Agreement to infer laws from common circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: By considering observed places (effects) as effects of a cause, find the circumstance in which observed instances agree; conclude that unobserved instances will share that circumstance (inferring a law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a set of observed effects agree in a particular circumstance (e.g., all lie on an ellipse), infer that the law governing the phenomenon includes that circumstance. Use careful comparison to identify the common property before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form conceptions by comparison and abstraction from phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions are obtained by abstraction from individual things through comparison; they may be evolved from the very facts they later colligate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the requisite conception pre-exists; be prepared to derive the needed general idea from the phenomena via careful comparison. Examples: conceiving 'white thing' or 'cloven-footed animal' through direct comparison; Kepler could only use an ellipse if the idea was already accessible or could be abstracted under suitable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure conceptions are appropriate to the object of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception is appropriate when it corresponds to a real agreement among the phenomena and is relevant to the particular object in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriateness is relative to purpose: e.g., classifying animals by color is appropriate for studying color causes but not for anatomy. Avoid selecting agreements that are trifling or irrelevant (Aristotle's 'towards its own place' is given as an inappropriate conception for motions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure conceptions are clear and determinate
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear conception means knowing exactly in what the agreement among instances consists; it is determinate, fixed, and not fluctuating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearness requires that we have analysed and memorably recorded the points of resemblance; it depends on attentive observation, extensive experience, and accurate memory. Do not use vague 'general feelings of resemblance' as bases for induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid erroneous or rash abstractions ('notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ')
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions wrongly formed are principal obstacles to good induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against forming abstract conceptions without sufficient grounding in the facts. Bad abstractions mislead subsequent induction; check abstractions against a wide set of instances and be ready to revise them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a tentative, iterative process for finding the right conception
rubrics_metrics.description: We find the right conception by a tentative process: trying one conception, comparing instances, changing path if unsatisfied, and generating different conceptions until one fits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a plausible type, test it against further instances, drop or modify it if it fails, and iterate. The fact that conceptions often manifest as something compared with phenomena during later stages explains why they may appear pre-existing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a type/standard to compare many objects during classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When arranging many objects, fix upon one object (or a type) as a standard and compare others to it; this process initiates abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a striking or representative example as the starting-point, then analyse agreements with subsequent objects to derive the conception. If the type fails, restart with a different exemplar or abstract to a more general conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to plurality of causes where no single law covers all cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some phenomena cannot be brought under one law because no agreement runs through all cases and no single conception is appropriate (a case of plurality of causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a class of phenomena (e.g., 'spontaneous motions') is heterogeneous; avoid forcing a unifying conception where multiple causes better explain the observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success of induction depends on observational skill and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal requisites of clear conceptions and thus of good induction are habits of attentive observation, extensive experience, and an accurate memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in improving observation and record-keeping practices; these faculties determine both clearness and the chance of hitting upon appropriate conceptions. Lack of these faculties leads to vagueness or inappropriate abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish deduction of particulars from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular propositions deduced from general propositions (e.g., deducing the earth is an oblate spheroid from measurements) are not inductions; they are deductions whose premises may themselves have inductive origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, separate deductive conclusions (which follow from premises) from inductive generalizations (which extend to unobserved cases). Avoid conflating the act of proposing a hypothesis with the act of inductive generalization.
